title: A service account key was pasted into a public gist
intro: GitHub secret scanning notified Google, and Google notified you: a JSON key for ci-deployer@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com (key id 3f9a1c2b4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c) appeared in a public gist 40 minutes ago. The account has roles/editor on production.

steps.prompt: Contain first: disable the leaked key 3f9a1c2b4d5e6f708192a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c on ci-deployer@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com (disable, keep it for the investigation).
Check what was done with it: read audit logs for activity by ci-deployer@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com in the last 2 hours.
steps.fake_output:
timestamp: '2026-09-28T11:02:40Z'  methodName: SetIamPolicy  callerIp: 45.155.205.10
  request: add member user:backup.admin.ops@mailbox.example role roles/owner
timestamp: '2026-09-28T11:03:12Z'  methodName: v1.compute.instances.insert  callerIp: 45.155.205.10
  resource: zones/asia-east1-a/instances/sys-helper-01 (a2-highgpu-8g)

steps.prompt: The attacker made an external personal account an Owner, which is persistence that survives disabling the key. Remove user:backup.admin.ops@mailbox.example from roles/owner on shop-prod-217733.
expected_commands: gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding shop-prod-217733 --member user:backup.admin.ops@mailbox.example --role roles/owner

steps.prompt: Stop the GPU instance sys-helper-01 the attacker launched in asia-east1-a (snapshot it later for forensics).
expected_commands: gcloud compute instances stop sys-helper-01 --zone asia-east1-a

steps.prompt: Check for other user-managed keys on ci-deployer@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com that the attacker could have created.
expected_commands: gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account ci-deployer@shop-prod-217733.iam.gserviceaccount.com --managed-by user

resolution: Same playbook as aws-incident-004, on GCP: contain the credential, then assume the attacker established persistence and hunt for it. The audit logs showed an external Owner binding and a second key created at 11:04 (still to be disabled), and either would have kept the attacker in after the original key was disabled. The GPU VM in an unused region is the usual crypto-mining signature. Remaining steps: disable the second key; review every IAM binding changed in the window; delete the VM after snapshotting its disk; check the other regions and projects the account could reach; and file an abuse report and billing adjustment with Google. Root causes: a downloaded key existed at all (CI should use Workload Identity Federation, which has no key to leak), and a CI account held roles/editor. The org policy iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation prevents the whole class of incident.
